To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the sparsity and the life time of the events in the data have an important impact on the recommendation algorithms, (2) the geographic features can help to improve the recommendation quality, (3) the co-participation of the users in the events is not as important as we thought and (4) the hybrid recommendation algorithms can provide better performance than the individual algorithms in some cases.

i) event-based social networks have a high sparsity problem that can not be easily overcome by using the traditional techniques for dealing with sparsity in collaborative recommendation; ii) events are short lived items that can only be consumed once; iii) the co-participation of the same users in multiple events can be used to improve the performance of recommendation systems; iv) the location where events take place can be used to enhance the quality of recommendation, but only if it is properly handled.

1) the sparsity of the data is not a problem for event recommenders; 2) the life-time of events is a very important feature for the design of event recommender systems and 3) the geographic features of events can help improve the recommendation quality.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following research questions: 1. What are the main characteristics of event data that should be taken into account when designing event recommenders?
the following questions: (1) How can we characterize the EBSN data? (2) What are the main challenges in event recommendation? and (3) Which algorithms are suitable for event recommendation?
understanding and exploiting the specificities of EBSN to improve the design of recommender systems for events.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, although the new item problem and the sparsity of EBSN are still challenging issues, the co-participation of the users in events, the geographic features and the events’ life time can be exploited to design more effective recommendation algorithms for this specific domain.
there are no silver bullets for this problem, but a combination of different approaches can lead to a better performance.
there is no single best algorithm for event recommendation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
event recommendation in EBSN is still a challenging problem, and that more research is needed to address its particular characteristics.
the new item problem and the sparsity of the data make the event recommendation scenario very challenging.
event-based social networks present some particularities that make the design of effective recommendation algorithms a challenging problem.
The main takeaway from our work is that
event recommender systems are quite different from the typical recommendation scenario.
the event recommendation scenario poses new challenges to the design of recommenders and that the use of collaborative information can be very effective to overcome the new item problem.
, despite the differences with respect to traditional recommendation domains, the same basic principles apply to event recommenders, with the only caveat of having to consider the new item problem.
